title: Active Directory & Identity Defense
tagline: Defend the identity plane: AD structure and trust, the attack techniques that target it, and the tiered hardening model that stops them.
disclaimer: Independent study material by Interstitium Labs. Not affiliated with or endorsed by any vendor. Confers no certificate.

domains.name: Active Directory & Identity Defense
domains.summary: How Active Directory works, how attackers abuse it, and how defenders harden it — from trust design to tiered administration and phishing-resistant authentication.

scenarios.title: Trust Falls Downhill
scenarios.situation: Your company acquires a smaller firm and creates a two-way forest trust between the two AD forests so users can access resources in both. A colleague says 'it's just like a VPN tunnel between the forests.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the most important thing to understand about that trust before relying on it?
choices: A forest trust is an authentication path, not a network tunnel — and in a two-way trust, compromise can flow either direction, so both forests' security postures matter.
The trust encrypts all traffic between the forests automatically.
The trust merges both forests into one domain.
Trusts are one-way by definition and cannot be reversed.
scenarios.why: A trust says 'I will honor your authentication decisions.' A two-way trust means both sides say it, so the security of each forest now depends on the other — a compromised admin in the acquired forest can authenticate into your resources. That is why trust design is a security decision first and a convenience decision second.
scenarios.hint: Who is really being trusted here — the network, or the other forest's administrators?
objectives: AD structure and trust: trust relationships

scenarios.title: The Schema Master Is Down
scenarios.situation: During a maintenance window the domain controller holding the Schema Master FSMO role is powered off for hardware replacement. Help desk asks whether anyone can install applications or change passwords until it returns.
choices: Normal operations continue — password changes and logons are handled by other DCs. Only schema modifications (like extending the schema for a new application) are blocked until the role holder returns.
Nothing works until the Schema Master is back; all authentication stops.
All five FSMO roles move automatically to another DC within minutes.
Users must be told to stop logging in until the DC is restored.
scenarios.why: FSMO roles are single-master operations for tasks that cannot safely happen on two DCs at once. The Schema Master only gates schema changes — a rare operation. Day-to-day work (logons, password changes, group membership) is multi-master and unaffected. Knowing which role gates which operation is the core FSMO skill; the five roles are Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, and Infrastructure Master.
scenarios.hint: Ask what the Schema Master actually does day-to-day — and what it only does once in a blue moon.
objectives: AD structure and trust: FSMO roles

scenarios.title: Service Account With an SPN and a Weak Password
scenarios.situation: A vulnerability scan flags a service account that has a Service Principal Name registered and a password that has not changed in six years. The account runs a legacy reporting tool nobody wants to touch.
scenarios.prompt: Why is this combination specifically dangerous?
choices: Any domain user can request a Kerberos service ticket (TGS) for that SPN and then crack it offline — Kerberoasting. The old password is the weak link, and the attack needs no privileges and leaves little noise.
Service accounts cannot be attacked because they are not interactive logons.
The danger is only theoretical; Kerberos tickets cannot be cracked offline.
The fix is to delete the SPN so the service stops working entirely.
scenarios.why: Kerberoasting works because TGS tickets are encrypted with the service account's password hash, and any authenticated user may request them. The attacker takes the ticket home and guesses the password offline — no lockouts, no alerts. Long-lived, weak service-account passwords plus SPNs are the classic setup. Defenses: long random passwords (managed service accounts rotate them automatically) and monitoring for unusual TGS requests.
scenarios.hint: What does the attacker walk away with, and what do they need it to decrypt?

scenarios.title: Pre-Auth Disabled 'For Compatibility'
scenarios.situation: An audit finds three user accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled — set years ago 'for compatibility' with an old application that is long gone. The accounts have normal user privileges.
scenarios.prompt: What attack does this enable, and what is the fix?
choices: AS-REP roasting: without pre-authentication, anyone can request the account's AS-REP response and crack it offline, no credentials required. Re-enable pre-authentication (the default) and rotate the passwords.
Nothing — pre-authentication is optional and disabling it is harmless.
It enables pass-the-hash, which is fixed by changing the domain functional level.
The accounts must be deleted; they can never be secured.
scenarios.why: Kerberos pre-authentication proves the requester knows the password before the KDC answers. With it disabled, the KDC hands out an encrypted AS-REP to literally anyone who asks for that username — and that blob is crackable offline. It is one of the cheapest account takeovers in AD: no privileges needed, just a username list. The fix is a checkbox (re-enable pre-auth) plus a password rotation.
scenarios.hint: What is the KDC giving away for free here, and to whom?

scenarios.title: The Help Desk Admin Problem
scenarios.situation: Your organization has 40 help desk staff who all hold Domain Admin 'because they sometimes need to reset things.' A tiered-administration proposal suggests Tier 0 (domain controllers, identity systems), Tier 1 (servers), and Tier 2 (workstations), with separate privileged accounts per tier.
scenarios.prompt: Why does the tiered model matter, and what is the first concrete change?
choices: It stops credential theft from spreading: an admin's credentials are only ever exposed on systems at their tier, so a compromised workstation cannot yield Domain Admin hashes. First change: remove standing Domain Admin from help desk and issue tier-appropriate accounts.
It is just paperwork; 40 Domain Admins is fine if they are trustworthy.
The first change should be renaming the Administrator account.
Tiering only matters for compliance audits, not real security.
scenarios.why: Pass-the-hash and token theft mean that wherever an admin logs on, their credentials become stealable on that machine. Forty Domain Admins logging into workstations means Domain Admin material sits on forty attack surfaces. Tiering enforces a simple rule: Tier 0 credentials never touch Tier 1 or Tier 2 systems. LAPS (unique local admin passwords per machine) and Credential Guard then shrink what is stealable at each tier.
scenarios.hint: If an attacker owns one help desk workstation today, what do they walk away with under the current model?
objectives: Hardening: tiered admin model, LAPS, Credential Guard

scenarios.title: DCSync From a 'Backup' Account
scenarios.situation: A routine review finds a service account with the 'Replicating Directory Changes All' permission on the domain — granted years ago to a backup product that was replaced. The account is still active.
scenarios.prompt: What is the risk, and what is the correct remediation?
choices: That permission lets the account impersonate a domain controller and pull password hashes via replication — the DCSync technique. Remove the permission (and the stale account), then audit who else holds replication rights.
It is harmless; replication permissions are read-only and cannot expose credentials.
The risk is only that backups fail; re-grant the permission to be safe.
DCSync requires Domain Admin, so a service account cannot perform it.
scenarios.why: DCSync abuses a legitimate replication right: ask the DC for changes 'as if' you were another DC, and it hands over hashes — including the krbtgt account's, which enables golden-ticket forgery. The permission is powerful by design and should exist on almost nothing. Stale grants to dead products are how attackers inherit domain-replication rights without ever touching an admin account. Audit replication rights regularly and treat any unexpected holder as an incident.
scenarios.hint: What is the account allowed to pretend to be, and what does a domain controller hand to its peers?

domains.name: AdFind & Active Directory Reconnaissance Hunting
domains.summary: How ransomware operators map Active Directory with the free AdFind query tool — and how defenders detect the recon, hunt it with behavior-based logic, and use its artifacts to rebuild the intrusion timeline.

scenarios.title: The recon that wore a helpdesk badge
scenarios.situation: Tuesday 09:14. Your EDR fires on WKSTN-214 in accounting: adfind.exe executed by marisol.vega, a standard user with no admin rights. The parent process is cmd.exe launched from a batch file. Command line: adfind -f (objectcategory=computer) -sc computers_pwdnotreqd > C:\Windows\Temp\c.txt. Marisol says she was ‘running a script IT sent her.’
evidence:
adfind.exe | parent: cmd.exe (recon.bat)
user: marisol.vega (standard, non-admin)
cmdline: adfind -f (objectcategory=computer) -sc computers_pwdnotreqd > C:\Windows\Temp\c.txt
Marisol has no admin duties. No change ticket references recon.bat. Two more adfind runs followed within 90 seconds: (objectcategory=person), then trustdmp.
choices: Close as benign: AdFind is a legitimate admin tool and Marisol says IT sent the script.
Escalate as suspected ransomware reconnaissance: non-admin user, batch wrapper, burst of discovery queries with output staged to Temp.
Block the adfind.exe hash enterprise-wide and close the alert.
Reimage the workstation immediately without further investigation.
scenarios.why: AdFind is dual-use: legitimate for admins, but a ransomware-affiliate recon staple. The discriminating facts are context, not the binary — a non-admin user, a batch wrapper, a burst of discovery queries (computers, people, trusts), and output staged to Temp. That pattern matches pre-ransomware AD mapping. Blocking the hash alone is theater, since the tool is trivially renamed, and reimaging destroys the forensic artifacts (those Temp output files) that anchor your timeline.
scenarios.hint: Ask what separates an admin's AdFind from an attacker's: who ran it, from where, how many queries, and where the output went.

scenarios.title: Three queries in ninety seconds
scenarios.situation: You are writing the detection for AdFind abuse. The SOC is drowning in noise: your first draft fired on every domain admin who ever ran the tool. You need logic that catches ransomware-affiliate recon while letting legitimate administration through.
scenarios.prompt: Which detection design is most defensible?
evidence:
A: any adfind.exe execution
B: 3+ distinct recon tokens (objectcategory=person/computer, trustdmp, dcmodes, computers_pwdnotreqd, ‘Domain Admins’) with output redirect (>) inside 2 minutes
C: adfind.exe only on domain controllers
D: command lines containing the word ‘trust’
choices: A: alert on any adfind.exe execution — simplest, catches everything.
B: burst of distinct recon query types plus output redirection in a short window, on hosts where the user is not a known admin — behavior over filename.
C: only monitor domain controllers — that is where AD lives.
D: match the substring ‘trust’ — trusts are the attacker’s real goal.
scenarios.why: Behavior beats filename: attackers rename binaries freely, so hash and name matching is brittle. The published hunting logic (Microsoft’s Defender query, Sigma’s win_susp_adfind) keys on distinctive command-line tokens — objectcategory filters, trustdmp, dcmodes, computers_pwdnotreqd — combined with output redirection and a burst threshold, scoped to unexpected users and hosts. That is what separates a ransomware affiliate’s recon batch from a domain admin’s one-off query, and it survives renaming.
scenarios.hint: What survives when the attacker renames adfind.exe to svchost.exe?

scenarios.title: The timestamps that moved the breach
scenarios.situation: During scoping you find C:\Windows\Temp\ad1.txt, ad2.txt, ad3.txt on a file server — AdFind outputs enumerating users, computers, and trusts. Their creation timestamps are 11 days older than your assumed initial-access date. Legal is drafting the breach notification on the old timeline.
scenarios.prompt: What do you do with these files?
evidence:
ad1.txt (users) — created 11 days before assumed initial access
ad2.txt (computers) — same day, 4 minutes later
ad3.txt (trusts) — same day, 9 minutes later
Initial access was estimated from the first EDR alert. No earlier evidence was found — until these files.
choices: Ignore them: text files in Temp are junk, and the EDR alert is the authoritative start.
Treat the AdFind output timestamps as the earliest hard evidence of recon, extend the intrusion window back 11 days, and tell legal the notification scope and deadlines may change.
Delete them to keep the timeline clean for the report.
Attribute them to a penetration test without checking for an engagement record.
scenarios.why: Recon output files are timeline anchors: they prove an attacker-controlled process was enumerating the domain on that date. Practitioners note these Temp-staged AdFind outputs are often the earliest hard evidence that recon began — which can push the whole intrusion timeline back. That changes dwell-time math, the scope of log review, and potentially breach-notification deadlines. Deleting them would be destruction of evidence; assuming a pen test without a record is wishful thinking.
scenarios.hint: What does a file creation timestamp prove that an alert timestamp doesn’t?

scenarios.title: Map the batch to ATT&CK
scenarios.situation: You recover the attacker’s recon batch file. It runs four AdFind passes: (objectcategory=person), (objectcategory=computer), -sc trustdmp, and a subnet enumeration. Your detection coverage map needs the ATT&CK techniques.
choices: All four are T1087 Account Discovery — discovery is discovery.
T1087.002 Domain Account, T1018 Remote System Discovery, T1482 Domain Trust Discovery, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery.
T1190 Exploit Public-Facing Application for all four — they came from the internet.
T1003 Credential Dumping — enumeration is a form of dumping.
scenarios.why: ATT&CK discovery techniques split by what is being discovered: domain accounts (T1087.002), remote systems (T1018), domain trusts (T1482), and network configuration (T1016). Mapping precisely matters because coverage maps, hunt hypotheses, and Sigma rules key off technique IDs — lumping everything under one ID hides gaps. T1190 is initial access, not discovery; T1003 is credential theft, a different tactic entirely.
scenarios.hint: Discovery techniques are named for the thing discovered. What four different things did the batch enumerate?

scenarios.title: Legit or lateral?
scenarios.situation: Two AdFind executions, same week. Case A: a domain admin runs AdFind from the admin jump host during a change window to audit stale computer accounts. Case B: a service-desk user runs it at 2:14 AM from a workstation, parented by a batch file, output to Temp. Same binary, same query syntax.
scenarios.prompt: Which contextual signals decide the triage?
choices: The binary hash — if it matches the known-good AdFind, both are benign.
Context: account privilege, host role, parent process, time of day, and output destination. Case B’s combination is the attacker pattern; Case A is administration.
The query syntax — attackers use different LDAP filters than admins.
Neither can be judged; AdFind is too common to triage.
scenarios.why: Dual-use tools are judged by context, not by binary. The hash is identical in both cases — it is the same legitimate tool. What differs is who ran it (privileged admin vs standard user), from where (jump host vs workstation), how (interactive audit vs batch wrapper at 2 AM), and where the output went. Train the SOC on that five-signal checklist and AdFind stops being either ‘always fine’ or ‘always evil’.
scenarios.hint: The binary is identical in both cases. So what isn’t?

scenarios.title: After the recon
scenarios.situation: AdFind reconnaissance is confirmed on a domain-joined host: users, computers, and trusts were enumerated six hours ago. No lateral movement alerts yet. The helpdesk wants to ‘just delete the tool and move on.’
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct immediate response?
choices: Delete adfind.exe from the host and close the ticket — tool removed, problem solved.
Isolate the host, preserve the Temp output files, hunt for lateral movement (PsExec, RDP, WMI), and scope which credentials and trusts the recon exposed — recon is the precursor, not the incident.
Force a password reset for every user in the domain immediately.
Wait for the ransomware to detonate so you have a confirmed incident.
scenarios.why: Recon is the precursor to lateral movement, not the whole incident: deleting the tool removes nothing the attacker needs (they can bring it back in seconds) and destroys your evidence. The correct sequence is isolate to stop the clock, preserve the recon outputs for timeline and scoping, then hunt the techniques that follow discovery — remote execution and lateral movement — because ransomware affiliates enumerate precisely so they can move next. Domain-wide password resets before scoping are disruptive theater; waiting for detonation is negligence.
scenarios.hint: Recon answers the attacker’s question ‘what can I reach next?’ — what do you do about the answer?

lessons.title: Active Directory & Identity Defense — Core concepts
concepts: AD structure: domains group into trees, trees into forests; trusts are authentication paths between them — two-way trusts mean compromise can flow either direction.
FSMO roles (Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master) serialize operations that cannot safely run multi-master; know which role gates which task.
Group Policy is the control plane: whoever can edit GPOs can push configuration — and malware — to every machine in scope.
Kerberoasting: any user can request crackable TGS tickets for SPN accounts — defend with long random service passwords and managed service accounts.
AS-REP roasting: accounts with pre-authentication disabled hand crackable responses to anonymous requesters — re-enable pre-auth (the default).
Pass-the-hash/ticket reuses stolen credential material without knowing the password; DCSync/DCShadow abuse replication rights to pull hashes — audit who holds 'Replicating Directory Changes All'.

Hardening: the tiered admin model keeps Tier 0 credentials off lower-tier systems; LAPS gives every machine a unique local admin password; Credential Guard isolates secrets; phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2) stops credential replay.

example.code:
# Hunt for the classic misconfigurations: SPN accounts with old passwords,
# and any account with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled.
# (Run from a domain-joined host with the RSAT AD PowerShell module.)
Import-Module ActiveDirectory
# 1. Accounts with pre-auth disabled (AS-REP roastable):
Get-ADUser -Filter { DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true } -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object Name, Enabled, PasswordLastSet
# 2. User accounts with SPNs set (Kerberoastable candidates):
Get-ADUser -Filter { ServicePrincipalName -ne '$null' } -Properties PasswordLastSet |
    Select-Object Name, PasswordLastSet
example.walkthrough: Defense starts with inventory: you cannot protect what you have not enumerated. The first query surfaces accounts with pre-authentication disabled — each one is an anonymous offline-cracking opportunity. The second lists accounts holding SPNs — the Kerberoasting surface. Both are one-line checks that belong in every AD security review, run before any hardening project begins.

pitfalls: Common trap: treating a trust as a network tunnel — it is an authentication relationship, and two-way means risk flows both ways.
Common trap: assuming only Domain Admins can DCSync — any account with replication rights can; audit the permission, not just the group.
Common trap: thinking Kerberos attacks need privileges — Kerberoasting needs only a valid domain user; AS-REP roasting needs no credentials at all.
Common trap: hardening servers while leaving 40 standing Domain Admins on workstations — tiering and LAPS address the credential-exposure path that attackers actually use.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: AdFind & AD Reconnaissance Hunting — Core concepts
concepts: AdFind is a free command-line Active Directory query tool (joeware) — a legitimate admin utility that ransomware affiliates adopted as a recon staple. It is dual-use, not malware, and notably absent from LOLBAS: defenders must detect its abuse, not its existence.

The classic recon query set: (objectcategory=person) and (objectcategory=computer) for accounts and hosts, -sc trustdmp / domainlist / dcmodes / adinfo for trust and domain topology, computers_pwdnotreqd for weak-password footholds, and ‘Domain Admins’ for the crown jewels. Each query answers one attacker question.

Detection is behavioral: process creation for adfind.exe (or its renamed twin) plus distinctive command-line tokens, output redirection (>), and a burst threshold — e.g., 3+ distinct query types in two minutes — on hosts and accounts where it is unexpected. Public coverage exists: Sigma (win_susp_adfind, win_ad_find_discovery), Elastic, Splunk, Sentinel, and Microsoft’s Defender hunting query.

Map precisely to ATT&CK discovery: T1087.002 Domain Account, T1069.002 Domain Groups, T1018 Remote System Discovery, T1482 Domain Trust Discovery, T1016 System Network Configuration Discovery. Precise mapping exposes coverage gaps.

Recon outputs are forensic gold: .txt files staged in Temp or staging folders carry creation timestamps that often predate every alert — the earliest hard evidence of when recon began. Extending the timeline can change log-review scope and breach-notification deadlines.
Triage on context: account privilege, host role, parent process (batch/cmd wrappers), time of day, and output destination separate the domain admin’s audit from the affiliate’s recon batch.

example.walkthrough: One line, three tells: an objectcategory discovery filter, a canned query for accounts that don’t require passwords, and output redirected to Temp. A domain admin auditing stale machines runs this from a jump host with a ticket; a ransomware affiliate runs it from a workstation at 2 AM inside a batch file. Same syntax — the context is the detection.

pitfalls: Common trap: blocking the filename or hash. Attackers rename adfind.exe freely — match on command-line behavior, not the binary name.
Common trap: alerting on every AdFind execution. Domain admins use it legitimately; without user/host scoping and a burst threshold, the rule is pure noise.
Common trap: ignoring the output files. Deleting Temp ‘junk’ during cleanup can destroy the earliest timeline anchor you have.
Common trap: treating recon as the incident. Discovery is the precursor — the response must hunt what comes next: lateral movement.
lessons.try_it: Open the Terminal tab and draft the Sigma detection for burst AdFind recon, then walk the timeline-reconstruction lab.

labs.title: AD Attack-Surface Audit
labs.objective: Enumerate the classic AD misconfigurations — pre-auth-disabled accounts, SPN-holding accounts with stale passwords, and holders of replication rights.
steps: List all accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled and note their last password change.
List all user accounts with SPNs registered and flag any with passwords older than one year.
Enumerate which security principals hold 'Replicating Directory Changes All' on the domain naming context.
For each finding, write a one-line risk note naming the attack it enables (AS-REP roasting, Kerberoasting, DCSync).
Prioritize the findings: anonymous-exploitable first, then user-exploitable, then privileged.
Draft the remediation order: re-enable pre-auth, rotate service passwords, remove stale replication grants.

checks.hint: Filter Get-ADUser on DoesNotRequirePreAuth -eq $true to find AS-REP-roastable accounts.
Run audit-repl to list holders of replication rights on the domain.

labs.title: Tiered Admin Design and GPO Lockdown
labs.objective: Design a tiered administration model for a fictional org and lock down Group Policy editing rights.
steps: Inventory the current privileged accounts and map each to Tier 0, 1, or 2 based on what systems they touch.
Identify every account with standing Domain Admin that only performs Tier 1 or Tier 2 work.
Design replacement accounts: one Tier 0 account per domain admin, separate Tier 1/Tier 2 admin accounts, no overlap.
Restrict GPO edit rights to Tier 0 and document which GPOs are security-critical (the control plane).
Specify LAPS deployment for workstation local admins and Credential Guard enablement via GPO.
Define the phishing-resistant MFA rollout order: Tier 0 first, then Tier 1, then all privileged users.

checks.hint: Run tiermap with your account list; it validates the tier assignments.
Run gpolock to verify GPO edit rights are restricted to Tier 0.

labs.title: Hunt AdFind Recon in Process Telemetry
labs.objective: Write behavior-based hunt logic that flags ransomware-affiliate AdFind reconnaissance while excluding legitimate admin use.
steps: Open the Terminal tab. You will draft hunt tokens; the terminal echoes each back into your rule draft.
Type exactly: objectcategory=person — the token for user enumeration.
Type exactly: trustdmp — the token for trust enumeration.
Type exactly: computers_pwdnotreqd — the token for weak-password-account discovery.
Type exactly: threshold 3 in 2 minutes — your burst condition across distinct tokens.
Review the assembled draft and write the exclusion in your notes: suppress only when the user is a documented admin AND the host is an admin jump host.

labs.title: Rebuild the Intrusion Timeline from Recon Artifacts
labs.objective: Use AdFind output-file timestamps to correct an intrusion timeline and state the notification impact.
steps: Three AdFind output files sit in C:\Windows\Temp on the file server: ad1.txt (users), ad2.txt (computers), ad3.txt (trusts).
Type exactly: ad1.txt created 11 days before first alert — record the earliest artifact.
Type exactly: timeline extended 11 days — state the correction to the intrusion window.
List what must now be re-reviewed: 11 more days of firewall, VPN, and authentication logs.
Write the notification note: the breach-notification deadline clock may restart from the earlier date — flag it for legal.
Document the preservation rule: image the host before any cleanup touches Temp.

checks.command_pattern: ad1\.txt created 11 days before first alert
checks.expect_contains: ad1.txt created 11 days before first alert
checks.hint: Record the earliest artifact: ad1.txt created 11 days before first alert.
State the correction: timeline extended 11 days.

sections.title: Active Directory & Identity Defense — defender path

behavioral.prompt: Explain Active Directory to a non-technical executive in two minutes.
behavioral.framework: Analogy first (the company's identity phone book plus its rulebook), then why it matters (everything authenticates through it), then the risk (compromise the directory, compromise everything).
points: Plain language, no jargon pile-up
Why AD security is business security
One concrete risk the executive should fund fixing
pitfalls: Reciting FSMO roles to a CFO
No business-impact framing

behavioral.prompt: Walk me through how you would respond to a suspected DCSync attack.
behavioral.framework: Contain → investigate → eradicate → recover: isolate the suspect account, audit replication-right holders, check for golden tickets (krbtgt password changes), rotate krbtgt twice, review logs.
points: krbtgt double-rotation as the golden-ticket killer
Audit of who held replication rights
Timeline built from DC event logs
pitfalls: Only disabling the suspect account and calling it done
Forgetting that forged tickets survive a password change until krbtgt rotates twice

behavioral.prompt: A legacy application requires a service account with a weak, unchangeable password. How do you handle it?
behavioral.framework: Risk acceptance with compensating controls: isolate the account, monitor its SPN, restrict logon rights, document the exception with an expiry.
points: Never accept silently — document and time-box
Compensating controls (isolation, monitoring)
A migration plan, even a slow one
pitfalls: Just saying no with no alternative
Accepting the risk permanently with no review date

behavioral.prompt: How do you convince reluctant admins to give up standing Domain Admin?
behavioral.framework: Empathy + evidence: show the credential-theft path, offer a better workflow (just-in-time elevation, tiered accounts), pilot with volunteers.
points: Demonstrate the attack path, not just the policy
Make the secure path the easy path
Measure and report reduced exposure
pitfalls: Leading with compliance mandates
Removing access with no replacement workflow

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you found a misconfiguration before an attacker did.
behavioral.framework: STAR: how you found it (audit, alert, curiosity), the risk it posed, how you fixed it, and what you changed so it stays fixed.
points: Proactive discovery, not incident-driven
Clear risk explanation
A systemic fix, not a one-off
pitfalls: A story where someone else found it
Fixing it with no preventive follow-up

behavioral.prompt: How do you prioritize: patching domain controllers, rotating service passwords, or deploying MFA?
behavioral.framework: Risk-based ordering: what is remotely exploitable now, what enables lateral movement, what has the broadest blast radius — then sequence and explain trade-offs.
points: Explicit risk model, not gut feel
Quick wins sequenced with structural fixes
Communication of the plan to stakeholders
pitfalls: Patching everything in no particular order
Ignoring the human/organizational constraints

behavioral.prompt: Describe a disagreement about identity architecture — for example, whether to add a forest trust.
behavioral.framework: STAR: the proposal, your security analysis, how you presented the trade-off, and the decision that resulted.
points: Security analysis in business terms
Alternatives proposed (selective authentication, one-way trust)
Respect for the final decision
pitfalls: Blocking without alternatives
Security absolutism that ignores business needs

behavioral.prompt: Where is identity security heading, and how are you keeping up?
behavioral.framework: Trends (phishing-resistant MFA, tiered privilege, cloud-hybrid identity) plus a concrete learning habit.
points: Awareness of phishing-resistant authentication
Understanding of hybrid identity challenges
Active learning: labs, reading, community
pitfalls: No opinion on where the field is going
Learning only when forced by an incident

cheatsheet: Forest → trees → domains. Trust = authentication path; two-way = risk flows both ways.
FSMO: Schema Master, Domain Naming Master, PDC Emulator, RID Master, Infrastructure Master. Single-master only for operations that cannot be multi-master.
GPO = control plane: who can edit GPOs can own every machine in scope.
Kerberoasting: any user requests TGS for SPN accounts → crack offline. Defense: long random passwords, managed service accounts, monitor TGS requests.
AS-REP roasting: pre-auth disabled → anonymous crackable response. Fix: re-enable pre-auth (default), rotate password.
Pass-the-hash/ticket: reuse stolen credential material without the password. Defense: Credential Guard, tiering, no credential reuse across tiers.
DCSync: replication rights abused to pull hashes. Audit 'Replicating Directory Changes All' holders; treat surprises as incidents.
Tiered model: Tier 0 creds never touch Tier 1/2 systems. LAPS: unique local admin password per machine. MFA: phishing-resistant (FIDO2) for privileged accounts.

glossary.def: The AD security boundary: one or more domain trees sharing schema and configuration. Compromise of the forest root compromises everything inside.
An authentication relationship between domains or forests; defines whose authentication decisions are honored.
Flexible Single Master Operations: five AD roles held by single DCs for operations that cannot run multi-master.
Service Principal Name: the Kerberos identifier for a service; accounts holding SPNs are Kerberoasting targets.
Requesting crackable Kerberos service tickets (TGS) for SPN accounts as any user, then cracking them offline.
Exploiting accounts with Kerberos pre-authentication disabled to obtain crackable responses without credentials.
Authenticating with a stolen password hash instead of the plaintext password.
Authenticating with a stolen Kerberos ticket, bypassing password authentication entirely.
Abusing domain replication rights to pull password hashes from a DC while impersonating another DC.
Registering a rogue DC to inject malicious replication changes into AD.
Separating privileged accounts into tiers (0: identity systems, 1: servers, 2: workstations) so credentials never cross tiers.
Local Administrator Password Solution: unique, rotating local admin passwords per machine.
Windows virtualization-based isolation of credential material so stolen hashes/tickets are harder to extract.
A forged Kerberos ticket-granting ticket using the krbtgt hash; killed by rotating krbtgt twice.

simulations.title: DCSync replication attack in progress
simulations.brief: The SIEM fires at 02:14: a non-domain-controller host is issuing DRS replication requests against DC02. Credential theft is underway right now. Work the response.

steps.symptom: Event 4662 audit shows Ds-Replication-Get-Changes rights exercised by SVC-backup from WS-114, which is not a domain controller.
options: DCSync attack: a compromised account with replication rights is pulling password hashes — treat as active credential theft
Normal backup traffic: the backup service legitimately replicates the directory
A misconfigured monitoring agent polling LDAP
Routine SYSVOL replication between domain controllers
evidence: 02:14:03 Event 4662 — Subject: SVC-backup — Object: DC=corp,DC=local — Accesses: DS-Replication-Get-Changes, DS-Replication-Get-Changes-All — Source host: WS-114
WS-114: finance workstation. Domain controllers: DC01, DC02 only. SVC-backup: backup service account, member of no replication-authorized group per policy.
steps.explain: Only domain controllers should issue DRS replication calls. A workstation exercising DS-Replication-Get-Changes is the textbook DCSync pattern — it pulls every password hash in the domain, including krbtgt.

steps.symptom: You must contain the attack without tipping off the intruder's persistence. What is the correct containment order?
options: Reset the krbtgt password first, then investigate
Isolate WS-114 from the network, disable SVC-backup, then hunt for additional footholds before any password resets
Delete the SVC-backup account immediately
Shut down DC02 to stop the replication
evidence: Containment: sever attacker access first (host isolation, account disable), THEN remediate credentials. Resetting krbtgt while the attacker still holds access lets them re-establish.
WS-114: active C2 beacon to 185.220.x.x every 60s.
steps.explain: Isolation plus account disable cuts the attacker's hands off first. Password resets come after you confirm the foothold is gone, or the attacker just re-steals the new hashes.

steps.symptom: WS-114 is isolated and SVC-backup disabled. The attacker held DCSync rights for ~40 minutes. What completes eradication?
options: Re-enable SVC-backup with a new password
Reset the krbtgt account password twice, force password resets for all privileged accounts, audit replication rights
Restore DC02 from last night's backup
Block port 445 on the firewall
evidence: Memory capture from WS-114 shows Mimikatz sekurlsa output. DCSync window: 01:34–02:14. Hashes for 1,900+ accounts exfiltrated, including krbtgt.
After krbtgt compromise: reset twice to invalidate both current and previous password (ticket lifetime overlap). Audit all principals with DS-Replication-Get-Changes.
steps.explain: With hashes exfiltrated, every derived ticket is suspect. The double krbtgt reset invalidates old and new ticket-granting tickets; privileged resets and a replication-rights audit close the loop.

simulations.debrief: DCSync turns any account with replication rights into a domain-wide password dump. Respond in order: confirm the anomaly, isolate the host and disable the account, hunt for footholds, then double-reset krbtgt and audit who holds replication rights. Prevention is least privilege on the directory itself.

simulations.title: Kerberoasting: hunting crackable service tickets
simulations.brief: Overnight the SIEM logged a burst of Kerberos TGS-REQ messages with RC4 encryption from a single workstation. A service account may be getting roasted. Investigate.

steps.symptom: 3,100 TGS requests in 20 minutes from WS-087, all requesting RC4-encrypted service tickets.
options: Likely Kerberoasting: bulk TGS requests for RC4 tickets are harvested for offline cracking
Normal service startup after a reboot
A backup job enumerating shares
DNS misconfiguration causing ticket retries
evidence: 00:41–01:02: 3,104 TGS-REQ from 10.4.8.87 (WS-087), etype rc4-hmac. No failures — valid user context.
Normal TGS rate per host: ~40/hour. RC4 usage fleet-wide: <1% of tickets.
steps.explain: Kerberoasting needs no privilege: any authenticated user can request service tickets and crack them offline. The volume plus forced RC4 downgrade is the signature — legitimate clients overwhelmingly negotiate AES.

steps.symptom: The tickets target MSSQLSvc/sql01.corp.local. What do you check next to confirm the exposure?
options: The service account's password age, complexity, and whether it is a managed service account
The SQL server's patch level
The workstation's antivirus status
The domain functional level
evidence: SVC-sql: password last set 2019-03-11 (7 years). Not a gMSA. Member of Domain Admins (legacy).
steps.explain: Kerberoasting succeeds against weak service-account passwords. A seven-year-old password on a Domain Admin service account is the jackpot: crack the ticket, own the domain.

steps.symptom: Confirmed: SVC-sql is roastable and over-privileged. What is the durable fix?
options: Disable Kerberos on the SQL server
Migrate to a group Managed Service Account with a long random password, remove Domain Admin, enforce AES
Rename the service account
Block RC4 at the firewall
evidence: gMSA: 240-char auto-rotated passwords, cannot be cracked offline practically. AES-only: removes the RC4 downgrade path. Least privilege: service accounts are never Domain Admins.
steps.explain: gMSAs remove the crackable secret entirely through automatic rotation of very long passwords, and AES-only kills the downgrade. Renaming changes nothing about the hash.

simulations.debrief: Kerberoasting is a defender's audit gift: it only works where service accounts are weak. Hunt for TGS volume anomalies, then fix the root cause — managed service accounts, long random passwords, AES enforcement, and least privilege.

simulations.title: Forged Kerberos tickets bypassing authentication
simulations.brief: A user account shows successful logons to servers it never touched, with ticket lifetimes of 10 years. Something is forging Kerberos tickets. Track it down.

steps.symptom: TGT lifetime 10 years for user j.chen; logons to FILE03 and BACKUP01 with no corresponding interactive session.
options: Golden ticket: forged TGTs signed with the stolen krbtgt hash, valid for years and invisible to normal logon auditing
A misconfigured SSO token cache
Clock skew between the workstation and the DC
Cached credentials from an old VPN session
evidence: TGT issued for j.chen with lifetime 87600h. Domain policy max: 10h. No 4768 (TGT request) precedes the 4769 service tickets.
No logon session for j.chen on FILE03 in EDR telemetry — the tickets arrive without authentication.
steps.explain: Golden tickets are minted offline with the krbtgt hash, so the KDC never logs a TGT request. Absurd lifetimes and logons with no authentication event are the tells.

steps.symptom: You suspect krbtgt compromise. How do you confirm the scope before remediating?
options: Check every host for malware
Correlate anomalous-lifetime tickets across DCs, identify when the krbtgt hash was first abused, and inventory accounts with replication rights
Force a password change for j.chen
Rebuild the affected file servers
evidence: Anomalous-lifetime TGTs seen on DC01 and DC02 since 2026-09-19. First abuse predates the j.chen sightings by three weeks.
Principals with DS-Replication-Get-Changes: Domain Controllers, SVC-backup, SVC-oldmigrator.
steps.explain: Scope first: the earliest forged ticket bounds the compromise window, and the replication-rights inventory shows every path the attacker could have taken to steal krbtgt.

steps.symptom: Scope confirmed: krbtgt hash stolen via the stale SVC-oldmigrator account. What is the remediation sequence?
options: Disable SVC-oldmigrator, reset krbtgt twice, reset all privileged passwords, remove stale replication rights
Reset krbtgt once and monitor
Demote and rebuild both DCs
Enable MFA on the VPN
evidence: krbtgt double-reset: two resets invalidate tickets minted under both the current and previous hash. Single reset leaves the previous-hash window open.
steps.explain: Kill the entry path, double-reset krbtgt to burn both ticket generations, rotate everything the stolen hash could have touched, and remove the stale rights so it cannot recur.

simulations.debrief: Golden tickets persist because defenders reset once or never. The discipline is: scope the abuse window, kill the theft path, double-reset krbtgt, rotate privileged credentials, and audit replication rights so the theft cannot repeat.

simulations.title: The legacy app that demands Domain Admin
simulations.brief: A vendor's legacy inventory app requires its service account to be a Domain Admin or it will not start. The business says it is critical. Decide the identity architecture.

steps.symptom: Vendor support insists: 'SVC-inventory must be Domain Admin. No workaround.' The app runs on one member server.
options: Grant Domain Admin — the business need outweighs the risk
Refuse outright and let the app stay broken
Profile the app's actual needs with auditing, grant only the specific rights it uses, isolate the server in a tier-appropriate OU with constrained delegation
Make it a local admin on the domain controller
evidence: Vendor requires 'Domain Admin or equivalent' — undocumented which privileges are actually exercised.
Tier 0 (domain controllers, identity systems): only Tier 0 admin accounts. Member servers: Tier 1. Workstations: Tier 2. No account crosses tiers.
steps.explain: Vendors ask for Domain Admin because it is easy, not because it is needed. Auditing reveals the true minimum — usually a handful of specific rights — and the tier model keeps those rights from reaching Tier 0.

steps.symptom: Auditing shows the app only writes to one OU and reads three attributes. The vendor still refuses to support a non-DA configuration. Your call?
options: Document the exact delegated rights, implement them, accept the support risk with business sign-off, and monitor the account as privileged
Give up and grant Domain Admin
Run the app on a domain controller so DA is 'contained'
Create a second Domain Admin as a backup
evidence: Residual risk: unsupported config. Mitigations: delegated rights documented, account monitored as Tier 1 privileged, server isolated, quarterly re-audit.
steps.explain: Security decisions are risk decisions with owners. Delegation plus monitoring plus documented business acceptance beats both blanket refusal (business harm) and surrender (domain-wide risk).

simulations.debrief: Standing Domain Admin for applications is how domains fall. Profile the real need, delegate precisely, enforce the tier boundary, and make the residual risk explicit and owned — never silent.

simulations.title: AdFind-style reconnaissance at 3 AM
simulations.brief: DC01 logs show thousands of LDAP queries enumerating group memberships and trust relationships from a helpdesk workstation at 03:00. Nobody works the helpdesk at 3 AM. Hunt it.

steps.symptom: 4,200 LDAP queries in 35 minutes from HD-022, enumerating 'Domain Admins', trusts, and GPOs. Source user: helpdesk intern account.
options: Active Directory reconnaissance: pre-attack enumeration mapping privileged groups, trusts, and policy — likely AdFind or similar tooling
The intern doing diligent after-hours study
A vulnerability scanner's scheduled run
Replication traffic misattributed to the workstation
evidence: 03:02–03:37: 4,213 queries from 10.4.9.22. Filters: (memberOf=CN=Domain Admins*), (objectClass=trustedDomain), (objectClass=groupPolicyContainer). Base DN: whole domain.
adfind.exe executed 03:01 from C:\Users\intern\Downloads. Parent: cmd.exe. No ticket for after-hours work.
steps.explain: Bulk enumeration of privileged groups, trusts, and GPOs with a dedicated recon binary is the attack-planning phase. Legitimate admin work is targeted; this is cartography.

steps.symptom: Recon confirmed on HD-022. What is the right next move?
options: Confront the intern immediately
Isolate HD-022, preserve memory and disk for forensics, reset the intern account credentials, and hunt for follow-on activity (lateral movement, persistence)
Delete adfind.exe and close the ticket
Block LDAP at the firewall
evidence: Recon is the precursor, not the payload. Assume the account is compromised until proven otherwise; hunt for what the recon was planning.
steps.explain: Recon means an attack is being planned — possibly by the account owner, possibly by someone who stole the session. Preserve evidence, kill the access, and hunt for the next phase instead of just deleting the tool.

simulations.debrief: LDAP recon is the attacker's map-making. Baseline normal query volumes, alert on bulk enumeration of privileged objects, and treat recon as the start of an investigation — not the end of one.

consoleSims.title: Work the DCSync SIEM alert
consoleSims.brief: Alert ALT-2077: 'DCSync replication from non-DC host WS-114'. Acknowledge it, assign it to the identity analyst, and escalate it to Tier 2.

tasks.hint: Click acknowledge on alert ALT-2077 in the SIEM queue.
Use the assign control on ALT-2077 and enter analyst r.okafor.
Click escalate on ALT-2077 to send it to Tier 2.

consoleSims.debrief: Identity-plane alerts are never low priority: acknowledge so nobody else duplicates the work, assign a named owner, escalate with the DCSync context attached.

consoleSims.title: Open the identity incident ticket
consoleSims.brief: Open a P1 incident ticket for the DCSync attack, assign it to the on-call identity responder, and move it to in-progress.

tasks.instruction: Create a P1 ticket titled 'DCSync attack from WS-114'.
tasks.hint: Create a ticket with title 'DCSync attack from WS-114' and priority P1.

consoleSims.debrief: Active credential theft gets a P1, a named owner, and a live status — the ticket is the shared picture while the response runs.

consoleSims.title: Cut off the rogue replication host
consoleSims.brief: WS-114 (10.4.8.114) is pulling directory replication traffic. Drop its SMB/replication traffic at the host firewall, then set the FORWARD chain default to DROP.

tasks.instruction: Add a rule dropping TCP port 445 from 10.4.8.114 on INPUT.
tasks.hint: Add an INPUT rule: protocol tcp, port 445, source 10.4.8.114, action DROP.

tasks.instruction: Set the FORWARD chain default policy to DROP.
tasks.hint: Set the default policy of the FORWARD chain to DROP.

consoleSims.debrief: Network containment buys time: drop the attacker's replication and C2 paths at the firewall while the host is isolated and credentials are rotated.

consoleSims.title: Lock down the offline AD backup
consoleSims.brief: The offline NTDS backup at /backups/ntds.dit is world-readable. Restrict it to root-only access.

tasks.instruction: Change the owner of /backups/ntds.dit to root.

consoleSims.debrief: An offline NTDS.dit is the whole domain in a file. World-readable backups are a DCSync without the network — permissions are a control, not paperwork.

terminalMissions.title: Find the recon queries
terminalMissions.brief: Search the LDAP query log for bulk enumeration of the Domain Admins group.
terminalMissions.success_message: Recon queries located — bulk enumeration of Domain Admins confirmed.

terminalMissions.title: Verify the AD backup integrity
terminalMissions.brief: Before restoring anything, verify the offline NTDS backup hash matches the known-good value.
objectives: Run sha256sum on ntds-backup.dit and confirm the filename in the output
terminalMissions.success_message: Backup hash verified — the offline copy is intact.

terminalMissions.title: Check domain controller SRV records
terminalMissions.brief: Confirm DNS still advertises the legitimate domain controllers via SRV lookup.
objectives: Dig the _ldap._tcp SRV record for the domain
terminalMissions.success_message: SRV records resolve to the legitimate domain controllers.

terminalMissions.title: Hunt SYSVOL for planted scripts
terminalMissions.brief: Attackers plant scripts in SYSVOL for GPO-based persistence. Find any PowerShell scripts there.
terminalMissions.success_message: SYSVOL sweep complete — planted scripts identified for review.

terminalMissions.title: Diff the Group Policy backup
terminalMissions.brief: Compare the known-good GPO export against the current one to spot unauthorized changes.
terminalMissions.success_message: Policy drift found — unauthorized GPO changes are now visible.

terminalMissions.title: Sort the failed logon list
terminalMissions.brief: Sort failed-logons.txt so you can spot the accounts under password-spray attack.
terminalMissions.success_message: Logons sorted — spray targets clustered for the hunt.

terminalMissions.title: Count the replication events
terminalMissions.brief: Count how many DRS replication events fired during the attack window.
objectives: Count lines in drs-events.log with wc
terminalMissions.success_message: Event count captured — the replication window is now quantified.
